title: Basic SecurityFilterChain Configuration
description: Configure a SecurityFilterChain bean for a REST API. The chain should: disable CSRF, set session policy to STATELESS, permit all requests to /auth/**, require authentication for everything else, and disable form login and HTTP Basic.
hints: Use .csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable()) for the lambda DSL style used in Spring Security 6
SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS is what you want for JWT APIs — it prevents any session from being created
Use .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth.requestMatchers(...).permitAll().anyRequest().authenticated())
Disable form login with .formLogin(form -> form.disable()) and HTTP Basic with .httpBasic(basic -> basic.disable())

solution.explanation: This is the foundational SecurityFilterChain configuration for a stateless JWT REST API. csrf().disable() is safe here because stateless APIs use JWT in the Authorization header, not cookies — so cross-site request forgery is not applicable. STATELESS session policy prevents Hibernate from creating HttpSessions, enabling true horizontal scalability. requestMatchers("/auth/**").permitAll() opens the login and registration endpoints without authentication. anyRequest().authenticated() serves as a catch-all, requiring authentication for any URL not previously matched. Disabling form login and HTTP Basic removes the default Spring Security login page and the basic auth challenge header.

methodSignatures.description: Configures CSRF protection; call csrf.disable() for stateless REST APIs
Configures session creation policy; STATELESS prevents session creation
Defines URL authorization rules evaluated in order
Finalizes and creates the SecurityFilterChain bean

title: Role-Based URL Authorization
description: Configure URL authorization rules with role-based access. Rules: GET /products/** is public, POST/PUT/DELETE /products/** requires ROLE_ADMIN, /user/profile/** requires ROLE_USER or ROLE_ADMIN, /admin/** requires ROLE_ADMIN, and the auth endpoints are public. Everything else must be authenticated.
hints: Use HttpMethod.GET as the first argument to requestMatchers() to restrict by HTTP method
hasRole('ADMIN') automatically checks for ROLE_ADMIN authority — the ROLE_ prefix is added for you
hasAnyRole('USER', 'ADMIN') checks for either role
Order matters! More specific rules must come before broader ones. /auth/** before anyRequest()

solution.explanation: requestMatchers(HttpMethod.GET, "/products/**") matches only GET requests to /products/**, leaving POST/PUT/DELETE to be matched by subsequent rules. hasRole('ADMIN') is equivalent to hasAuthority('ROLE_ADMIN') — Spring Security prepends the ROLE_ prefix automatically when using hasRole(). hasAnyRole() checks if the user has at least one of the listed roles. The critical insight: rules are evaluated top-to-bottom and the FIRST matching rule wins. If you placed anyRequest().authenticated() before the /admin/** rule, the admin rule would never be reached. Always order from most specific to least specific.

methodSignatures.description: Matches requests by HTTP method AND path pattern
Requires ROLE_ + role authority; equivalent to hasAuthority('ROLE_' + role)
Requires at least one of the listed roles
Matches any request not matched by previous rules; must be last

title: Implement UserDetailsService
description: Implement a UserDetailsService that loads a user from a UserRepository by username. Return a UserDetails object with the user's username, password, and roles mapped to GrantedAuthority objects. Throw UsernameNotFoundException if the user doesn't exist.
hints: Use userRepository.findByUsername(username).orElseThrow(() -> new UsernameNotFoundException(...))
Map each role string to new SimpleGrantedAuthority(roleName)
Spring Security's built-in User class (org.springframework.security.core.userdetails.User) implements UserDetails — use its constructor
The User constructor takes: username, password, enabled, accountNonExpired, credentialsNonExpired, accountNonLocked, authorities

solution.explanation: UserDetailsService is the bridge between Spring Security's authentication mechanism and your user storage. loadUserByUsername is called by DaoAuthenticationProvider during login. The UsernameNotFoundException message is technically visible in the 401 response for Spring Security's default behavior; to prevent username enumeration attacks in production, throw a generic AuthenticationException or configure hideUserNotFoundExceptions = false carefully. SimpleGrantedAuthority is the standard GrantedAuthority implementation for string-based roles. The boolean flags in the User constructor represent account status checks — all true here for simplicity, but in production these would check database flags like isEnabled, isAccountNonExpired, etc.

title: PasswordEncoder Bean and Registration
description: Define a BCryptPasswordEncoder bean with a cost factor of 12. Write a register method in an AuthService that encodes the user's password before saving and throws an exception if the username is already taken.
hints: BCryptPasswordEncoder constructor accepts an integer strength (cost factor); 12 is a good production value
userRepository.existsByUsername(username) or findByUsername().isPresent() to check existence
passwordEncoder.encode(rawPassword) returns the BCrypt-hashed string
Never call passwordEncoder.matches() during registration — that's only for login verification

solution.explanation: BCryptPasswordEncoder(12) sets the work factor to 12, meaning 2^12 = 4096 BCrypt iterations. This makes brute-force attacks expensive while still completing in under 300ms on modern hardware. As hardware improves, increase this factor. The passwordEncoder is a @Bean so it can be injected both here and into DaoAuthenticationProvider (which uses it to verify passwords during login). The raw password is NEVER stored — only the BCrypt hash. Each call to encode() produces a different hash for the same password because BCrypt generates a random salt internally; this is by design and why you use matches() for verification rather than comparing hash strings directly.

methodSignatures.description: Creates encoder with given work factor (4-31); 10-12 is recommended for production
Hashes the raw password with a random salt; produces a 60-character BCrypt string
Verifies raw password against the stored hash; used internally during login by DaoAuthenticationProvider

title: Configure AuthenticationManager with DaoAuthenticationProvider
description: Configure a DaoAuthenticationProvider using your CustomUserDetailsService and BCryptPasswordEncoder, then expose an AuthenticationManager bean. Write a login method that uses AuthenticationManager to authenticate and returns the Authentication object on success.
hints: DaoAuthenticationProvider has setUserDetailsService() and setPasswordEncoder() methods
To expose AuthenticationManager as a bean: define a method with AuthenticationManagerBuilder parameter and call builder.authenticationProvider(daoProvider).build()
UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken.unauthenticated(username, password) is the factory method for the pre-auth token in Spring Security 6
AuthenticationManager.authenticate() throws AuthenticationException (BadCredentialsException, etc.) on failure — let it propagate

solution.explanation: DaoAuthenticationProvider is the bridge between Spring Security's authentication model and your user storage. It calls userDetailsService.loadUserByUsername(), gets the UserDetails, then calls passwordEncoder.matches(submittedPassword, storedHash). Only if both succeed does it create a fully authenticated Authentication object. The AuthenticationManager bean is exposed so it can be injected into controllers/services for programmatic authentication (like a login endpoint). UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken.unauthenticated() is the Spring Security 6 API for creating a pre-authentication token — the older new UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken(u, p) two-arg constructor still works but is less expressive.

title: JwtUtil — Generate and Validate Tokens
description: Implement a JwtUtil utility class that generates JWT tokens (with username, roles, iat, and exp claims) and validates them. Use the jjwt library (io.jsonwebtoken). The signing key is injected from application.properties as a Base64-encoded string.
hints: Use Decoders.BASE64.decode(base64Secret) then Keys.hmacShaKeyFor(bytes) to get the SecretKey
Jwts.builder().subject(username).issuedAt(new Date()).expiration(...).claim('roles', roles).signWith(key).compact()
Jwts.parser().verifyWith(key).build().parseSignedClaims(token).getPayload().getSubject() to extract claims
Wrap the parse in try-catch for JwtException and IllegalArgumentException to return false on any failure

solution.explanation: The signing key must be at least 256 bits (32 bytes) for HS256. Storing it as a Base64 string in application.properties (never in source code!) and decoding at runtime is the standard pattern. Keys.hmacShaKeyFor() creates a type-safe SecretKey from the raw bytes. Jwts.builder() uses the fluent jjwt API — subject(), issuedAt(), and expiration() set the registered claims; claim() adds custom claims like roles. parseSignedClaims() performs full validation: signature check, expiry check, and malformed-token check in one call. Catching JwtException (parent of ExpiredJwtException, SignatureException, MalformedJwtException) and IllegalArgumentException covers all failure modes. In production, log the specific exception type at DEBUG level for troubleshooting.

methodSignatures.description: Builds and serializes the JWT to a compact URL-safe string
Parses and fully validates a signed JWT; throws JwtException on any failure
Returns the 'sub' claim value
Returns a custom claim cast to the specified type

title: JwtAuthenticationFilter — Protect Every Request
description: Implement JwtAuthenticationFilter extending OncePerRequestFilter. It should: extract the Bearer token from the Authorization header, validate it using JwtUtil, load the UserDetails, and set the Authentication in the SecurityContextHolder. Skip processing if no token is present.
hints: request.getHeader("Authorization") gets the header; check != null && startsWith("Bearer ")
Check SecurityContextHolder.getContext().getAuthentication() == null before processing
new UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken(userDetails, null, userDetails.getAuthorities()) — null credentials since JWT already verified
authToken.setDetails(new WebAuthenticationDetailsSource().buildDetails(request)) adds IP/session info

solution.explanation: OncePerRequestFilter guarantees exactly one execution per request, even in dispatcher-include or forward scenarios. The null/Bearer check is the first gate: requests without a JWT token (like public endpoints) pass through immediately without any processing — no unnecessary work. The SecurityContext null check prevents re-processing if another filter (or a nested dispatch) already set authentication. Passing null as credentials to UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken is correct for JWT: credentials were the token, already validated by jwtUtil — there's no need to re-expose the password. The three-argument constructor (principal, credentials, authorities) creates a trusted, already-authenticated token. Always call filterChain.doFilter() at the end — if you forget, the request is swallowed and no response is returned. The try-catch ensures invalid tokens result in a 401 (unauthenticated context hits the AuthenticationEntryPoint) rather than a 500.

methodSignatures.description: Override this method; guaranteed to run exactly once per request
Three-arg constructor creates an already-authenticated token (isAuthenticated() returns true)
Sets the Authentication for the current request thread
Passes control to the next filter; MUST be called to avoid swallowing the request

title: Register JWT Filter in Security Chain
description: Update the SecurityFilterChain to add the JwtAuthenticationFilter before UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter. Also wire in a custom AuthenticationEntryPoint for 401 responses and configure the full security chain for a JWT REST API.
hints: http.addFilterBefore(filter, FilterClass.class) places your filter before the specified filter type
http.authenticationProvider(provider) registers the auth provider directly on HttpSecurity
exceptionHandling(e -> e.authenticationEntryPoint(entry).accessDeniedHandler(handler)) configures both exception handlers
DaoAuthenticationProvider needs setUserDetailsService() and setPasswordEncoder()

solution.explanation: addFilterBefore(jwtAuthFilter, UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter.class) places the JWT filter at the right position in the chain: after SecurityContextPersistenceFilter (which sets up the empty context) but before UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter (which would try form-based login). This ordering ensures JWT tokens are validated before any default authentication attempt. The exceptionHandling configuration is critical for REST APIs: without it, Spring Security's default behavior for 401 is to redirect to /login — completely wrong for an API. The custom handlers return JSON bodies. authenticationProvider() is called so Spring Security knows which provider to use when AuthenticationManager.authenticate() is called from your login controller.

methodSignatures.description: Inserts a filter before the specified filter type in the security filter chain
Registers an AuthenticationProvider with the security filter chain's AuthenticationManager
Configures handlers for 401 (AuthenticationEntryPoint) and 403 (AccessDeniedHandler)

title: Method Security with @PreAuthorize
description: Enable method security and annotate service methods with @PreAuthorize. Implement: getAllUsers (admin only), getUserById (admin or the user themselves), updateUser (only the user themselves), and deleteUser (admin only). Use SpEL expressions.
hints: Add @EnableMethodSecurity to your SecurityConfig or a dedicated @Configuration class
hasRole('ADMIN') checks for ROLE_ADMIN authority in the SecurityContext
authentication.principal.id references the id field on your custom UserDetails implementation
authentication.name returns the username (equivalent to authentication.principal.username)

solution.explanation: @EnableMethodSecurity (replacing deprecated @EnableGlobalMethodSecurity) activates the AOP interceptors that process @PreAuthorize annotations. The SpEL expression runs before the method — if it evaluates to false, Spring throws AccessDeniedException (403) without executing the method. #userId == authentication.principal.id is an ownership check: #userId refers to the method parameter named userId (requires -parameters compiler flag, which Spring Boot enables by default), and authentication.principal is your UserDetails object — its id field is accessed directly. Note that principal.id requires your UserDetails implementation to have a public getId() method. authentication.name is equivalent to principal.username. The compound hasRole('ADMIN') or #userId == ... allows either admins or the resource owner to access their own data.

methodSignatures.description: Enables @PreAuthorize, @PostAuthorize, @PreFilter, @PostFilter; place on a @Configuration class
Evaluates SpEL expression before method execution; throws AccessDeniedException if false
Evaluates after method returns; has access to returnObject variable

title: Custom AuthenticationEntryPoint (401 JSON Response)
description: Implement a CustomAuthenticationEntryPoint that returns a JSON error response with HTTP 401 when an unauthenticated request hits a protected endpoint. The JSON body should contain 'status', 'error', 'message', and 'timestamp' fields.
hints: response.setStatus(HttpServletResponse.SC_UNAUTHORIZED) sets the HTTP 401 status code
response.setContentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE) sets the Content-Type header
objectMapper.writeValue(response.getWriter(), errorBody) serializes a Map to JSON
Use Map.of() or a LinkedHashMap to build the error body with the required fields

solution.explanation: AuthenticationEntryPoint.commence() is called by ExceptionTranslationFilter when an AuthenticationException is thrown — meaning the request is unauthenticated. The 401 status code (SC_UNAUTHORIZED) is semantically correct for 'not authenticated'. Setting Content-Type to application/json is essential for REST API clients that expect JSON — without it, clients may misinterpret the response. Using ObjectMapper (Spring's auto-configured Jackson instance) ensures consistent JSON formatting with your application's settings. Including the request path helps clients and developers identify which endpoint triggered the error. Note: this entry point is also triggered when a JWT token is expired or malformed — your JwtAuthenticationFilter catches JwtException and simply doesn't set the SecurityContext, so the request arrives at ExceptionTranslationFilter as unauthenticated.

title: Custom AccessDeniedHandler (403 JSON Response)
description: Implement a CustomAccessDeniedHandler that returns a JSON 403 Forbidden response when an authenticated user tries to access a resource they're not authorized for. Include the username of the denied user in the response.
hints: response.setStatus(HttpServletResponse.SC_FORBIDDEN) sets HTTP 403
SecurityContextHolder.getContext().getAuthentication().getName() gives the username
The AccessDeniedException message is 'Access is denied' by default — use a friendlier message
Include request.getRequestURI() to show which path was forbidden

solution.explanation: AccessDeniedHandler.handle() is called when an authenticated user is denied access due to insufficient authorities — the user is known (authenticated) but forbidden. This is fundamentally different from 401: a 403 response means 'I know who you are, but you can't do this.' Including the username in the response helps audit logs and debugging while not exposing sensitive data (the user knows their own username). The Optional.ofNullable guard around getAuthentication() is defensive coding — in practice, AccessDeniedHandler is only called for authenticated users, but it prevents a NullPointerException in edge cases. Never include stack traces or internal error details in the 403 response body — those should go to server logs only.

title: CORS Configuration for React Frontend
description: Configure CORS for a Spring Boot API that serves a React frontend at http://localhost:3000 (development) and https://myapp.com (production). Allow common HTTP methods, the Authorization header, and credentials. Register the CORS config in the SecurityFilterChain.
hints: CorsConfiguration config = new CorsConfiguration(); config.setAllowedOrigins(List.of(...))
allowCredentials = true + specific origins (NOT *) — can't combine credentials with wildcard origin
UrlBasedCorsConfigurationSource registers the config for a URL pattern using source.registerCorsConfiguration("/**", config)
http.cors(cors -> cors.configurationSource(corsConfigurationSource())) wires CORS into the security chain

solution.explanation: CORS must be configured via Spring Security's cors() DSL rather than @CrossOrigin or a WebMvcConfigurer alone — Spring Security's CorsFilter needs to process CORS before authentication filters, otherwise preflight OPTIONS requests fail authentication and are rejected. allowCredentials(true) is necessary for the browser to include the Authorization header in cross-origin requests — but this combination requires explicit origins (not '*') because the spec prohibits wildcard origins with credentials. setMaxAge(3600L) tells browsers to cache the preflight response for 1 hour, reducing the number of preflight requests. In production, read allowed origins from @Value-injected properties rather than hardcoding them, enabling different origins per deployment environment.

title: OAuth2 Resource Server with Custom Role Extraction
description: Configure a Spring Security OAuth2 Resource Server that validates JWTs. The JWTs come from an Authorization Server and contain roles in a custom claim 'user_roles'. Configure a JwtAuthenticationConverter to map this custom claim to ROLE_* GrantedAuthority objects.
hints: .oauth2ResourceServer(oauth2 -> oauth2.jwt(jwt -> jwt.jwtAuthenticationConverter(converter())))
JwtGrantedAuthoritiesConverter allows setting .setAuthoritiesClaimName('user_roles')

Wrap JwtGrantedAuthoritiesConverter in JwtAuthenticationConverter and set it as the granted authorities converter

solution.explanation: oauth2ResourceServer().jwt() registers BearerTokenAuthenticationFilter, which extracts Bearer tokens and validates them using a JwtDecoder. When issuer-uri is configured, Spring Boot auto-creates a NimbusJwtDecoder that fetches the Authorization Server's JWKS endpoint to retrieve public keys — handling key rotation automatically. JwtGrantedAuthoritiesConverter maps JWT claims to GrantedAuthority objects. By default it reads the 'scope' or 'scp' claim with 'SCOPE_' prefix; we override both to match our custom token structure. JwtAuthenticationConverter wraps this into the Spring Security JwtAuthenticationToken (a subtype of AbstractAuthenticationToken). Setting the principal claim to 'sub' means authentication.getName() returns the subject claim — typically the user ID.

title: Custom Security Bean for Complex Business Rules
description: Create a custom Spring Security bean called 'documentSecurity' that checks ownership and sharing rules. Use it in @PreAuthorize expressions to protect service methods: users can read a document if they own it or it's been shared with them; only admins can delete documents.
hints: Name the bean 'documentSecurity' with @Component("documentSecurity") or via @Bean method
@PreAuthorize("@documentSecurity.canRead(authentication, #docId)") — @ prefix references a Spring bean
For update: check authentication.name equals the document's owner username
canDelete can be as simple as: auth.getAuthorities().stream().anyMatch(a -> a.getAuthority().equals("ROLE_ADMIN"))

solution.explanation: The @ symbol in @PreAuthorize SpEL expressions references a Spring bean by name. This is the recommended pattern for any business-rule-based security logic: keep your @PreAuthorize annotations readable and delegate complex checks to a dedicated, testable security service. The canRead method queries the database to check ownership and sharing — this is a legitimate DB query in a security context. The canDelete method uses pure authority checking without a DB call. The owner-check approach avoids loading the entity twice (once in the security check, once in the business method) at the cost of a potentially redundant DB call — profile before optimizing. An alternative is @PostAuthorize with returnObject for cases where you need the loaded entity for authorization: @PostAuthorize("returnObject.ownerUsername == authentication.name").

title: Authentication vs Authorization
description: What is the difference between authentication and authorization in Spring Security? When does each happen, and how are they represented in the framework?
hints: Think about WHO vs WHAT CAN
Where does Authentication object fit in? What about GrantedAuthority?
Which filters/components handle each?

solution.explanation: Authentication and authorization are the two core concepts in Spring Security. Authentication establishes identity — it answers 'who is this user?' by verifying credentials. The result is stored as an Authentication object in the SecurityContextHolder. Authorization then decides what the authenticated user can do — it checks the GrantedAuthority list against the required permissions. The separation is fundamental to the architecture: authentication providers are pluggable (you can have JWT + form login simultaneously), and authorization rules are expressed separately in SecurityFilterChain config and @PreAuthorize annotations. The 401 vs 403 response codes reflect this distinction: 401 means 'tell me who you are first', 403 means 'I know who you are but you can't do this.'

title: Why Disable CSRF for REST APIs?
description: Interview question: Why do we typically disable CSRF protection for stateless JWT REST APIs? What is CSRF, how does Spring Security protect against it, and why is it unnecessary for JWT APIs?
hints: CSRF exploits the browser's automatic cookie behavior
JWT is stored in memory or localStorage, not cookies
The Same-Origin policy prevents malicious sites from reading your JWT

solution.explanation: CSRF is a browser-level vulnerability that exploits the automatic sending of cookies. The browser's behavior of attaching cookies to every request, regardless of origin, is the root cause. Spring Security's CSRF token mechanism breaks this by requiring a secret value that only the legitimate origin can provide. However, this mechanism is irrelevant for JWT APIs because JWTs live in JavaScript-accessible storage (localStorage) or memory, not cookies. Since evil.com's forged request won't include the JWT Authorization header (the browser doesn't automatically attach custom headers to cross-site requests), the API simply sees an unauthenticated request and returns 401. Disabling CSRF removes unnecessary overhead and eliminates the need to handle CSRF tokens in your React/Angular frontend.

title: SecurityFilterChain Internals
description: Interview question: Explain how Spring Security's filter chain works internally. What is DelegatingFilterProxy, FilterChainProxy, and SecurityFilterChain? How does a request flow through them?
hints: Start with the Servlet container and how DelegatingFilterProxy bridges to Spring
FilterChainProxy holds multiple SecurityFilterChain instances
How does Spring select which SecurityFilterChain to apply?

solution.explanation: The layered architecture is designed for separation of concerns: the Servlet container knows about filters but not Spring; DelegatingFilterProxy bridges them; FilterChainProxy applies the correct chain per URL; SecurityFilterChain contains the actual security logic. The ability to have multiple SecurityFilterChain instances per application is powerful — microservices can have different security rules per API version or path. The key insight for interviews: Spring Security is entirely implemented as Servlet filters, not Spring MVC interceptors — it protects at the Servlet layer, before DispatcherServlet even sees the request.
